analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal aid to career programs that leave students with heavy debt, and restores loan forgiveness for students misled by colleges.
analysis.headline: The PROTECT Students Act was introduced March 12, 2025, and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has seen no hearing, no markup, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law rules requiring career education programs to show their graduates can earn enough to pay back their loans, and it would cut off federal aid to programs that fail those tests. It would make it easier to cancel student loans when a school lied or misled students, automatically cancel loans when a school closes, ban colleges from forcing students into arbitration or holding transcripts hostage over unpaid balances, and require colleges to spend at least 30% of tuition revenue on actual instruction. It would also create an enforcement office at the Department of Education and a complaint-tracking system for students to report problems.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and borrowers hurt by predatory career education programs — people left with large loan debt and little to show for it — get clearer warnings, easier loan cancellation, the right to sue, and protection from schools keeping transcripts hostage. Taxpayers also benefit because loan discharges from failed schools become recoverable from the institutions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students and borrowers at weak career programs

how_it_helps.text: Programs training students for a recognized occupation would lose federal aid eligibility if their graduates' debt-to-earnings rates are too high or their earnings are no better than a high school graduate's, after failing in 2 of any 3 consecutive years [S2] [S3].

The bill gives borrowers a statutory right to loan discharge when a school made a substantial misrepresentation, used aggressive or deceptive recruiting, or broke its promises, and requires the Department of Education to process widespread misrepresentation claims as a group [S2] [S3].

Borrowers whose school closed would be entitled to automatic discharge one year after closure without applying, and the Secretary could extend the coverage window when a school was already under sanction or quietly shut its campuses while keeping online programs [S3].

The bill bars institutions from forcing students to accept arbitration or other limits on suing in court, prohibits withholding official transcripts over a balance owed, and creates a private right of action with attorney's fees and up to threefold punitive damages for substantial misrepresentations [S2] [S3].
Colleges would have to spend at least 30% of net tuition and fee revenue on instruction, with the threshold revisited after five years of reported data [S2] [S3].

The bill establishes an enforcement unit inside the Office of Federal Student Aid with subpoena-backed investigations and 'secret shopping' of schools, a cross-agency For-Profit Education Oversight Coordination Committee, and a centralized complaint tracking system with published annual data [S2] [S3].

Civil penalties for misrepresentation would rise from $25,000 to $100,000 per violation or 1% of an institution's federal student aid take, and each time a misrepresentation is viewed could count as a separate violation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Career education programs — disproportionately for-profit colleges — that fail the debt-to-earnings and earnings tests would lose access to federal student aid and could not re-qualify for three years. Every institution taking federal aid would carry new reporting, attestation, and compliance duties, and loan discharges shift costs to the federal government until recouped from the institutions themselves.
analysis.who_pays_short: Failing career programs and for-profit colleges

drawbacks.text: The 30% instructional-spending floor applies to every institution receiving federal aid, not just weak ones, so well-run colleges and nonprofits would take on new reporting and compliance work to prove how they allocate revenue [S3].

Programs that fail the standards lose federal aid entirely and cannot re-establish eligibility for three years, which could leave some students — including those already enrolled — without access to that specific training, even if the program had some value [S3].

Borrower defense and closed-school discharges discharge the full loan balance including interest and fees, a cost the federal government absorbs up front; the bill relies on recouping those funds from the institutions, which may not be possible if the school is defunct [S3].

Administrative costs for operating the student aid programs — including the new enforcement unit — would be paid from funds not otherwise appropriated, capped at 5% of the outstanding student loan portfolio each year [S3].

The bill instructs agencies to carry out several provisions without going through the usual negotiated rulemaking process in section 492 of the Higher Education Act, which would speed implementation but reduce the procedural input institutions and other stakeholders normally get [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For students at predatory programs, the protections are substantial: real consequences for programs that leave graduates with unpayable debt, easier loan cancellation after fraud or closure, and the right to sue instead of being forced into arbitration. The main honest costs are regulatory burden on all colleges from the spending and reporting rules, reduced access to any failing program that still had some value, and up-front federal cost for discharges that may not be fully recovered from defunct schools. On balance the bill is aimed squarely at a documented harm — graduates of weak programs carrying debt they cannot repay — and its costs fall mostly on the programs causing it, though its one-size-fits-all compliance burden is a fair criticism.

outcome.mechanism: Read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote scheduled since.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on March 12, 2025, joined by Senators Warren and Merkley [S1] [S3] [S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S2] [S5].
The action history shows no further steps after the referral — no hearing, no committee report, no floor action [S5].
The bill has 2 cosponsors, both Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has been decided yet, so no one has won or lost through this bill. If it continues to sit without a hearing, the outcome preserves the status quo, under which career education programs that leave graduates with unpayable debt keep access to federal student aid and borrowers who were misled carry the burden of proving their claims case by case.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; bill stalled in committee

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.role: Sector targeted by the bill's gainful employment, enforcement, and oversight provisions
against.what_they_did: For-profit colleges and their trade groups have historically lobbied against gainful employment rules and borrower defense regulations of the kind this bill would codify into statute.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors are Democrats and the bill has no Republican cosponsors; it sits on the agenda of a committee now chaired by a Republican, and there has been no committee or floor action since referral.

industries.industry: For-profit colleges and career education providers
industries.note: The bill is aimed directly at this sector: programs whose graduates cannot earn enough to repay their loans would lose federal aid, misrepresentation would trigger loan discharges and penalties of up to $100,000 per violation or 1% of federal aid received, and a dedicated cross-agency committee would coordinate oversight of the sector. Its business model of recruiting students with aggressive tactics and charging high tuition against weak outcomes would be directly threatened.

The bill bars institutions from knowingly employing owners, directors, officers, or employees with substantial control who ran institutions that committed fraud or lost federal funds, and requires owners to personally sign agreements to repay liabilities assessed against their schools. It also revokes a 2011 guidance exception that had loosened the ban on incentive-based recruiter pay.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and third-party servicers
industries.note: Servicers and contractors would fall under the new enforcement unit, the complaint tracking system with mandatory response deadlines, and expanded civil penalties, and institutions could be penalized for their contractors' violations. Some programs managed by third-party servicers would face accreditor risk reviews.

Accreditors would face a new duty to assess risk to students, including programs run by third-party servicers, and to monitor quality — more obligations, but applied to a sector where accreditors have been criticized for lax review.

The 30% instructional-spending requirement, spending disclosures separating instruction from marketing and lobbying, and ban on transcript withholding apply to all institutions receiving federal aid, adding compliance work. Most established institutions already spend well above 30% on instruction and do not withhold transcripts, so their core operations are largely unaffected.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding the Senate majority and the HELP Committee chair, a bill with no Republican cosponsors that has sat without a hearing since its introduction is very unlikely to move this Congress; the most probable path is that it expires at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote, as similar previous iterations of this legislation have.
